issues.issue: The date, the Buyer's name, entity type and address are all left blank, so the instrument does not identify on its face who the Buyer is or when it was made. A court asked to enforce it would have to construe extrinsic material to fill those blanks.

"Approximately 10.89 acres" and the reference to Exhibit A leave the exact extent of the parcel to the exhibit, and "parcel!" is a scanning artifact. The acreage qualifier alone is a thin basis for dispute.

Section 1 conveys the parcel as legally described in Exhibit A, while Section 3 requires a deed containing "new legal descriptions" reflecting the City's plat of vacation of Sixth and Abbott Streets and the contiguous properties thereby created. What is sold under Section 1 and what is conveyed under Section 3 may not describe the same land.

"Standard deductions and prorations" is defined only by the parenthetical "customary closing expenses incurred by the Seller," leaving the boundary of what may be deducted from the $8,000,000 uncertain. "Customary" supplies no measurable benchmark.

The clause makes the remaining balance payable "less any deductions identified below" and "or less dependent upon setoffs as described below," but no deductions or setoffs are identified anywhere below in the Agreement. The size of the Outstanding Balance therefore cannot be computed from the text.

Nothing elsewhere in the instrument — §10 Default, §9 Prorations or §28 Tax Incentive Financing — supplies the promised setoff or deduction mechanism this clause points to. The Agreement read as a whole leaves the cross-reference dangling.

Interest accrues "to the same extent, if any," as the City or State pay interest on "the outstanding incurred eligible expenses," a term used nowhere else and never defined. Whether and at what rate the Seller earns interest cannot be determined from the words.

This sentence is duplicated verbatim as the last sentence of §28, except that §28 says "less any setoff" where this says "less any deductions," and the earlier part of §2 speaks of "setoffs as described below." The two near-identical operative sentences use different reduction concepts, neither defined.

Section 3 defines "Permitted Exceptions" by reference to an undated Real Estate Option Agreement, while §4 speaks of "those Permitted Exceptions attached hereto" and the attachment list carries "Exhibit B — Permitted Exceptions." The two sources of the defined term may not match.

The Title Company's office and location are left blank and the delivery deadline runs from "the date of this Agreement," which the preamble leaves undated. The commitment deadline therefore has no fixed starting point.

"Seller ... shall have ten (10) business days prior to the date of Closing" can be read either as a ten-business-day cure period ending at Closing or as a deadline falling ten business days before Closing. The difference decides when Seller's cure right expires.

Buyer must elect "prior to the expiration of the period for Seller to remedy," but the period fixed in the preceding sentence of §4 ("ten (10) business days prior to the date of Closing") is itself indeterminate. Buyer's election window cannot be dated without construing that sentence.

No date or deadline is fixed for Seller's delivery of the updated plat of survey, the trigger being only that the agreement "shall have been executed." The garbled "as a prepared in accordance with the 2005 ALTA standards" compounds the uncertainty.

Buyer's acceptance of the Property subject to all environmental laws and conditions sits against §7(d) and §7(e), in which Seller makes affirmative environmental representations and warrants them continuously true. Whether the acknowledgment defeats those representations is a genuine question.

"Except as expressly set forth elsewhere in the Agreement" carves out an unidentified body of other terms, and its reach across §7's representations is unclear. The exception's scope has to be construed against the whole document.

Buyer's agreement to take the Property in its closing-date condition "including all faults ... whether now or hereafter existing" cannot be squared with §11, which places risk of loss on Seller until deed delivery and requires Seller to repair injury or reduce the price. The two clauses assign post-signing deterioration to opposite parties.

"No knowledge of any reason why the local governmental authorities would not allow the Property to be developed for the Federal Office facilities contemplated herein" is a knowledge qualifier over an undefined development standard. What counts as a "reason," and whose knowledge, is left open.

Section 7(c) omits gas and qualifies utility availability "for its current use," whereas §26 makes the same representation as to gas and without that qualifier. The two representations about the same utilities do not say the same thing.

"All environmental information that it has" is bounded only by Seller's own possession, with no time or materiality limit, and "including the existence of asbestos containing materials" may or may not exhaust the subject. The scope of what had to be disclosed is uncertain.

The environmental representations are qualified "Except as otherwise indicated on Schedule A attached," but no Schedule A exists; the attachment list contains only Exhibit A (legal description) and Exhibit B (permitted exceptions). The carve-out from these representations therefore has no identifiable content.

Warranting the representations "will continue to be true and correct on each day hereafter" is unlimited in time and sits against §23, which fixes survival at completion of improvements and GSA's written acceptance of occupancy. The two survival periods differ.
The outside closing date runs "ninety (90) days after the execution of this Agreement," but the execution date is left blank in the preamble. The deadline has no ascertainable start.

This clause requires Buyer to cause "the Purchase Price" — $9,000,000 under §2 — to be paid at Closing, while §2 makes only $8,000,000 payable at Closing with the $1,000,000 balance payable out of future TIF receipts. Whether the tag "as provided for in Section 2" cures the discrepancy is a question of construction.

This is clause 8(a)(iv), yet its last sentence limits "This Section 8(a)(v)," which is the separate possession clause; the phrase "if required the Title Company" also drops a word. The mis-numbering leaves it unclear which obligation the extraordinary-obligations limit attaches to.

This clause splits "the charges of the Title Company" equally, while §4 puts the Title Commitment and policy "at Seller's sole cost and expense." Which Title Company charges fall on Seller alone and which are shared is left unresolved.
"All real estate taxes, expenses and charges in connection with ownership and use of the Property" is an open-ended category with no list to bound it. What is prorated is left to argument.

Buyer's remedies here are confined to specific performance (barred after ninety days) or actual damages, but the closing sentence of §10 says "the parties may seek any other remedy available at law or in equity." Whether the enumerated remedies are exclusive is squarely open.

The clause fixes "liquidated damages not to exceed $50,000" in the form of a letter of credit or cash to be posted "upon the execution of this Agreement and within ten (10) business days of Award and Assignment of the Option to Purchase" — two inconsistent posting dates — and misspells "letter" as "fetter." When the security is due, and whether the $50,000 is a cap or a fixed sum, cannot be read off the text.

A capped liquidated-damages remedy against Buyer cannot be reconciled with the last sentence of §10, permitting "any other remedy available at law or in equity." Whether Seller's recovery is limited to $50,000 turns on that conflict.

On revocation of the Assignment "the Buyer is entitled to the $50,000 letter of credit or cash equivalent," which reads oddly given that the same $50,000 is the security Buyer itself posts under the preceding sentence. Whether this is a return of Buyer's own security or a payment from Seller is ambiguous.

"Any subsequent Buyer" is nowhere defined and the sentence purports to impose an obligation on someone who is not a party, keyed to "the execution of this Agreement" that a subsequent buyer would not have executed. Who is bound, and when, is unclear on the face of the words.

This catch-all allowing "any other remedy available at law or in equity" cannot be squared with the preceding sentences of §10, which cap Seller's recovery at $50,000 in liquidated damages and confine Buyer to specific performance or actual damages. One reading nullifies the enumerated remedies.
